synopsis: ACARP is the Australian coal industry's levy-funded research fund; Mining3 delivered its C26028 proximity-detection testing framework in January 2021 as a shared physical-test protocol, not a simulator [f15625, f15626, f15627, f16088]. The framework proves object detection in Tier 1 before testing Level 8 or Level 9 advisory or intervention in Tier 2, providing comparability and credible independent evidence alongside other industry frameworks [f15628, f15630]. Its baseline covers only limited choreographed scenarios and excludes pre-existing site controls and complex, multi-variable vehicle interactions, so independent review cannot alone establish site-specific performance [f15629, f1055]. The booklet recommends this structure for physical testing after high-throughput regression, covering stopping performance, grades, loads, nuisance braking and other adverse conditions; for a team starting in October 2026, procedures, soft targets, ground-truth specifications and independent-body engagement are considered realistic by mid-2027 [f15634, f749, f851]. Separately, the University of Queensland's C24028 advisory-interface study ran in 2017 with follow-on work to 2019, using a modified haul-truck simulator; richer schematic displays reduced collision risk, braking force and travel time, but this was advisory-warning research rather than automatic-braking validation [f15631, f15632, f13405]. The booklet treats that study as its main off-road evidence for operator-in-the-loop testing, while an acceptable false-alarm rate remains an explicit unresolved research question [f15635, f15633, f3605].
